age.peak: bimodal: young children and older adults

demographics: Very common worldwide; affects all ages
Young children and older adults account for most severe cases
Outbreaks occur in closed settings such as daycare centers, nursing homes, cruise ships and camps

risk_factors.text: Contact with a person who has diarrhea or vomiting
Eating undercooked or improperly stored food, or drinking untreated water
Poor hand hygiene or crowded living conditions
Recent travel to an area with poor sanitation
Age under 5 years or over 65 years

social_history: Residence in a nursing home or other group setting
exposures: Sick contacts with vomiting or diarrhea
Suspected foodborne illness (restaurant meal, buffet, raw or undercooked foods)

chief_complaints.text: I feel nauseated and can't keep anything down

hpi.onset: Sudden, over hours, often after a known exposure or sick contact
hpi.duration: Typically 1–3 days for viral causes; up to 1 week or longer for some bacterial or parasitic causes
hpi.progression: Nausea and vomiting often come first, followed by watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain; symptoms peak over 1–2 days and then gradually improve
hpi.location: Diffuse abdominal pain, often periumbilical or lower abdomen
hpi.quality: Crampy, intermittent abdominal pain; watery, non-bloody stools
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; cramping 4–6/10, worst just before a bowel movement
hpi.timing: Cramps come in waves and ease after passing stool; diarrhea several times a day
pertinent_negatives: Blood or mucus in the stool
Severe localized right lower quadrant pain
Pain that started before any vomiting or diarrhea
Weight loss or chronic diarrhea lasting weeks

argues_against: Severe dehydration with altered mental status
Systemic vasculitis or other rash-associated illness

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot report symptoms; they present with irritability, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, no tears when crying and lethargy. Vomiting and diarrhea may be the only signs.
missing_classic_features: Verbal report of nausea or cramps

atypical.how_it_differs: May have milder diarrhea and fever but dehydrate quickly; confusion or falls may be the presenting problem.
Diarrhea can be prolonged, more severe and caused by opportunistic organisms; systemic symptoms may be more prominent.
Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance can affect the pregnancy; listeriosis should be considered with fever and flu-like symptoms.

general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, thirsty, slightly dry mucous membranes, mild tachycardia
general.severe: Ill-appearing, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, delayed skin turgor, lethargic or irritable
general.critical: Toxic or obtunded, profoundly dehydrated, hypotensive, mottled or cool extremities

labs.caveat: Rises with dehydration and prerenal azotemia; a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 supports volume depletion.
Rises late in dehydration; a normal value does not exclude significant volume loss.
Hyponatremia from losses replaced with free water; can also be hypernatremic if water intake is poor.
Hypokalemia from stool and vomit losses; check before giving fluids and replace as needed.
Low bicarbonate reflects bicarbonate loss in stool and metabolic acidosis.
Hypoglycemia in poor intake, young children and older adults; check point-of-care glucose in anyone ill-appearing.
Mild leukocytosis is nonspecific; marked leukocytosis or a left shift raises concern for invasive bacterial infection.
Elevated lactate with hypotension or mottling suggests hypoperfusion and warrants resuscitation.
Nonspecific; a high value or rising trend supports an inflammatory or invasive bacterial cause.
May help distinguish bacterial from viral gastroenteritis but is not routinely needed.
High specific gravity supports dehydration; a urinalysis also helps exclude a urinary source.
From poor intake and vomiting; not specific for gastroenteritis.
Negative. Check in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from dehydration, fever or pain
Sinus rhythm; may show occasional premature atrial or ventricular beats with electrolyte disturbance
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves with hypokalemia
ST depression with severe hypokalemia
Prolonged QT interval with hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia
Nonspecific ST-T changes from electrolyte derangement

findings.text: Nonspecific gas pattern with scattered air-fluid levels; no dilated bowel or free air

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When a surgical or inflammatory cause is suspected and the diagnosis is unclear

findings.text: Diffuse small and large bowel wall thickening with mural edema
Mesenteric fat stranding and mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy

imaging.preferred_when: Children and pregnancy when appendicitis, biliary disease or an ovarian cause is considered

findings.text: No dilated appendix, gallstones or ovarian abnormality

initial.why: Assesses dehydration, sodium, potassium, bicarbonate and kidney function; guides fluid and electrolyte replacement
Detects hypoglycemia, especially in children and frail older adults
Looks for leukocytosis or anemia that would suggest another diagnosis
initial.only_if: moderate to severe illness, fever, blood in stool or concern for a bacterial cause

initial.why: Excludes a urinary tract infection and assesses hydration
initial.only_if: dysuria, flank pain or concern for a urinary source

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before imaging or medication choices
Identifies bacterial pathogens when invasive disease is suspected
initial.only_if: bloody or mucoid stools, high fever, severe illness, recent travel or immunocompromise
recent antibiotic use, hospitalization or persistent diarrhea
prolonged diarrhea over 7 days, recent travel or untreated water exposure

initial.test: Rapid stool antigen or PCR panel for viral and bacterial pathogens
initial.why: Rapidly identifies common viral and bacterial causes
initial.only_if: moderate to severe illness or when a specific pathogen would change management

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory or invasive bacterial process when elevated
Assesses hypoperfusion in severe dehydration or sepsis
May help distinguish bacterial from viral gastroenteritis
supporting.only_if: diagnosis remains unclear and antibiotic decisions depend on it
severe abdominal pain, distension or concern for obstruction

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.why: Excludes a surgical or inflammatory cause when the presentation is atypical
supporting.only_if: severe or localized pain, peritoneal signs or an unclear diagnosis

supporting.why: Evaluates for appendicitis, biliary disease or an ovarian cause
supporting.only_if: localized right lower quadrant pain, right upper quadrant pain or pelvic symptoms

not_indicated.why: Not needed in mild, uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis
Not routine in mild watery diarrhea without red flags
Not routine without antibiotic exposure or persistent symptoms
Not routine in short-duration watery diarrhea

not_indicated.test: Rapid stool antigen or PCR panel for viral and bacterial pathogens
not_indicated.why: Not routine in mild self-limited illness
Rarely changes management in uncomplicated gastroenteritis

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed when the history and exam fit uncomplicated gastroenteritis
Not needed without localization or concern for another organ
Not needed unless pain is epigastric or radiates to the back

decision_points: Assess hydration first; oral rehydration is preferred when the patient can drink and is not severely dehydrated
Check a pregnancy test before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy
Order stool studies only when red flags are present: bloody or mucoid stools, high fever, severe illness, recent travel, antibiotic use or immunocompromise
Consider a surgical cause when pain is localized, precedes diarrhea or is accompanied by peritoneal signs
Consider C. difficile in anyone with recent antibiotic use or hospitalization

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
differential.why_considered: Watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain, often with recent healthcare exposure or antibiotics
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic use, hospitalization or persistent diarrhea after antibiotics

history: Antibiotics within the past 8 weeks
Recent hospitalization or nursing home stay
Diarrhea persisting or worsening after antibiotics were stopped
exam: Fever and systemic illness may be more prominent
labs: Positive stool C. difficile toxin or PCR
Elevated creatinine and lactate in severe colitis
imaging: Colonic wall thickening, thumbprinting or ascites on CT in severe disease
Toxic megacolon with colonic dilation in fulminant cases

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain that can mimic gastroenteritis, especially in children
differential.trigger: Pain that starts and localizes before diarrhea, or focal right lower quadrant tenderness

history: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant
Pain precedes vomiting and diarrhea
Anorexia with low-grade fever
exam: Focal right lower quadrant tenderness with rebound or guarding
Positive psoas, obturator or Rovsing sign
imaging: Non-compressible appendix greater than 6 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal or flank discomfort can be mistaken for gastroenteritis

history: Dysuria, urgency or frequency
Flank pain or fever with chills
No sick contacts or food exposure
labs: Positive urinalysis with leukocyte esterase, nitrites and pyuria
imaging: CT or ultrasound showing hydronephrosis or renal abscess if complicated

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease flare
differential.why_considered: Chronic or recurrent diarrhea with abdominal cramping and systemic symptoms

history: Diarrhea lasting weeks to months
Weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, or blood in stool
Prior diagnosis of Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis
exam: Oral ulcers, perianal disease or abdominal mass
imaging: Bowel wall thickening, skip lesions or fistulas on CT or MRI enterography

differential.name: Mesenteric ischemia
differential.why_considered: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and diarrhea, particularly in older adults with vascular risk factors
differential.trigger: Pain out of proportion to exam, older adult with atrial fibrillation or vascular disease

history: Sudden, severe, constant abdominal pain
Pain out of proportion to physical findings
Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction or peripheral vascular disease
exam: Diffuse tenderness with relatively benign initial exam
Peritoneal signs late in the course
imaging: CT angiography showing arterial occlusion, venous thrombosis or pneumatosis

differential.name: Food poisoning or toxin-mediated gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Acute vomiting and diarrhea shortly after eating, often with a common food source

history: Onset within hours of a specific meal
Multiple people affected after the same food
Vomiting predominates with short duration
exam: Diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs
labs: Usually normal or mild electrolyte abnormalities
Stool studies negative unless a specific pathogen is identified

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting in a sexually active patient

history: Vaginal discharge, dyspareunia or abnormal bleeding
New or multiple sexual partners
Pain worse with intercourse
imaging: Thickened fallopian tubes, fluid-filled tubes or tubo-ovarian abscess on ultrasound

severity.mild: Self-limited watery diarrhea and cramping with no dehydration, able to tolerate oral fluids, no fever or low-grade fever, normal mental status
severity.moderate: Frequent diarrhea and vomiting with mild dehydration, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, reduced oral intake, and mild electrolyte abnormalities
severity.severe: Marked dehydration with sunken eyes, delayed skin turgor, hypotension or significant tachycardia, electrolyte derangements, and inability to keep fluids down
severity.critical: Hypovolemic shock with hypotension, mottled or cool extremities, altered mental status, severe metabolic acidosis, or suspected sepsis

red_flags.finding: Blood or mucus in the stool
red_flags.meaning: Suggests invasive bacterial infection, inflammatory bowel disease or another serious cause; warrants stool studies and close follow-up
May indicate invasive bacterial infection or systemic illness; consider blood and stool cultures

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain or peritoneal signs
red_flags.meaning: Raises concern for a surgical abdomen such as appendicitis, perforation or ischemia

red_flags.finding: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, hypotension, confusion)
red_flags.meaning: Requires immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation and monitoring
Suggests a parasitic, bacterial or non-infectious cause and warrants further stool testing
Raises concern for Clostridioides difficile colitis

red_flags.finding: Inability to keep any fluids down
red_flags.meaning: Leads to progressive dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; may need IV fluids and antiemetics

complications.name: Dehydration and hypovolemia
clues: Thirst, dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output

complications.name: Acute kidney injury from prerenal azotemia
Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome
clues: Persistent altered bowel habits after resolution of acute illness

special_populations.differences: Cannot report symptoms; present with irritability, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, no tears when crying and lethargy. Dehydrate rapidly; lower threshold for IV fluids and hospitalization.
Higher risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; rotavirus and norovirus are common. Use oral rehydration solutions and monitor for lethargy or sunken eyes.
May have milder diarrhea and fever but dehydrate quickly; confusion or falls may be the presenting problem. Higher risk of complications and mortality.
Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance can affect the pregnancy; listeriosis should be considered with fever and flu-like symptoms. Avoid unsafe medications and ensure adequate hydration.
Diarrhea can be prolonged, more severe and caused by opportunistic organisms; systemic symptoms may be more prominent. Lower threshold for stool studies and hospitalization.

key_questions.question: How many times a day are you having diarrhea, and how long has it been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over hours to a few days with frequent watery stools; duration over 7 days or more than 6 stools a day suggests a more serious cause

key_questions.question: What do the stools look like — are they watery, or is there blood, mucus or pus in them?
key_questions.looking_for: Watery, non-bloody stools support viral gastroenteritis; blood, mucus or pus raises concern for invasive bacterial infection or inflammatory bowel disease

key_questions.question: Did the vomiting come before or after the diarrhea started?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting first followed by diarrhea fits gastroenteritis; pain that starts and localizes before any diarrhea suggests a surgical abdomen

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it stay in one spot or move around?
key_questions.looking_for: Diffuse, crampy, periumbilical or lower abdominal pain that comes in waves; focal right lower quadrant pain suggests appendicitis

key_questions.question: Have you been able to keep fluids down, and how much are you urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to keep fluids down, decreased urine output, dark urine or thirst indicates dehydration and need for IV fluids

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, and how high has it been?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade fever is common; a fever above 102°F raises concern for invasive bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you — family, daycare, work, school — had similar vomiting or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts support a viral or person-to-person cause; multiple people after the same meal suggests food poisoning

key_questions.question: What have you eaten or drunk in the last day or two, including restaurant meals, buffets, raw or undercooked foods, or untreated water?
key_questions.looking_for: A common food source or recent travel to an area with poor sanitation points to a foodborne or travel-associated pathogen

key_questions.question: Have you taken any antibiotics or been in the hospital recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Antibiotics within the past 8 weeks or recent hospitalization raises concern for Clostridioides difficile colitis

key_questions.question: Do you have any conditions or medications that weaken your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, chronic kidney disease, diabetes or inflammatory bowel disease increases risk of severe or prolonged illness

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes pregnancy-related causes and guides safe medication and imaging choices

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, flank pain, vaginal discharge or bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in gastroenteritis; present suggests urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis or pelvic inflammatory disease

key_questions.question: Any black tarry stools, severe localized pain, confusion, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Red flags for gastrointestinal bleeding, surgical abdomen or severe dehydration requiring urgent evaluation

reasoning_points: Acute onset of watery, non-bloody diarrhea with nausea, vomiting and crampy diffuse abdominal pain
Preceded or accompanied by a sick contact, suspect food or water exposure, or travel history
Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without focal right lower quadrant tenderness, guarding or rigidity
Signs of dehydration such as dry mucous membranes, tachycardia or reduced urine output when moderate to severe
Stool studies reserved for red flags: bloody or mucoid stools, high fever, severe illness, recent travel, antibiotic use or immunocompromise
Pregnancy excluded when relevant before imaging or medication choices
Surgical and inflammatory look-alikes considered and excluded by history, exam and targeted testing

easy: Young child or adult with a clear sick contact and acute watery diarrhea
Vomiting followed by diarrhea with diffuse crampy pain
Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs
No blood in stool and no high fever
medium: Older adult with milder diarrhea but significant dehydration and confusion
Recent antibiotic use raising concern for Clostridioides difficile
Patient with fever and bloody stools requiring stool studies
Woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain and gynecologic look-alikes
hard: Infant with irritability, poor feeding and no wet diapers, unable to report symptoms
Immunocompromised patient with prolonged or severe diarrhea from an opportunistic organism
Pregnant patient with fever and flu-like symptoms where listeriosis must be considered
Severe pain out of proportion to exam in an older adult suggesting mesenteric ischemia
Presentation after perforation or with toxic megacolon and systemic toxicity
